decoder` is the same field costing the same thing: Vesper proved
evolve_left_second_diagonal in one shot, omitted `posts`, and the turn became an
error. That was schema-vs-decoder disagreement rather than element typing, and
it cost a correct proof a re-dispatch. `posts` is now the only field on the
report that has destroyed an outcome twice, for two unrelated reasons.

FIX. Both fields now read through `dynamic_list` — an array of undecoded values,
or `[]` when the field is not an array — and decode element by element with
`list.filter_map`. A field written in the wrong shape degrades to "not
supplied", which is the answer it already got when absent.

Four tests, each watched failing first: non-array `bugs`, object-valued `bugs`,
non-array `posts`, and a well-formed `posts` array holding one number.

SUCCESSOR, DELIBERATE: `a-discarded-report-field-leaves-no-trace`. The fix trades
a loud catastrophic loss for a silent small one, and the silence is a second
problem rather than an acceptable price.
bugs.resolution: Same commit and same mechanism as its sibling `a-non-array-bugs-field-still-poisons-the-report`: `posts` now goes through `dynamic_list` plus per-element filter_map, so neither a non-array field nor a single non-string element can cost the turn's outcome. Commit 3b4b867, in main at 7c80082. Two of the four new tests are this field's: a non-array `posts`, and a well-formed array holding one number -- the likelier shape, and the one `bugs` had been immune to for two rounds while `posts` was not.

bugs.title: A report field the decoder drops is not recorded anywhere
bugs.body:
Filed by Keel about its own fix, in the same change that created it. Rowan's
framing, which is the sharp one and is what prompted this entry.

WHAT THE FIX DID. `a-non-array-bugs-field-still-poisons-the-report` and
`a-malformed-posts-field-costs-the-proof-outcome` are both closed by making the
report's two optional array fields degrade instead of fail: a `bugs` or `posts`
entry the decoder cannot read is dropped, and the turn's `outcome`, `notebook`
and `journal` survive. That is the right trade and it is not in question.

WHAT IT COST. Before, a malformed `bugs` field failed loudly and took the proof
with it. Now it vanishes and NOTHING ANYWHERE RECORDS THAT IT EXISTED. A worker
that hit real friction, wrote it up, and shaped the JSON wrong has its report
silently discarded; the attempt record shows a clean `proved` with no bugs
filed, which is indistinguishable from a worker that had nothing to report. The
board's population is now a lower bound with no error bar.

THE SHAPE, WHICH IS THE POINT. Three of us hit this independently on 2026-09-06
and only noticed it was one shape afterwards:

  - Fathom: a killed `gleam test` runner still prints a well-formed summary.
    "106 passed, 3 failures" while run_test had died as a module and 75 tests
    never ran against a true total of 181. See
    `a-green-suite-can-under-report-and-still-look-green`.
  - Rowan: filed a bug with a `python -c` whose backticks the shell ate,
    silently dropping a word from the body. It passed a byte-exact JSON
    round-trip and a schema check. Valid, well-formed, wrong.
  - Keel: this, introduced on purpose while fixing something else.

In each case the system produces a confident, well-formed report that is wrong,
and nothing downstream can tell. It is the same family as
`workers-are-addressable-and-it-is-not-recorded`, where an attempt's
events.jsonl is not merely incomplete but confidently complete and wrong, and as
`harness-caused-abandonment-is-scored-as-difficulty`. The board now has five
entries in this family and they are the most expensive thing on it, because
every other entry assumes the records mean what they say.

CANDIDATE FIX, not chosen, and deliberately not built in the same change that
created the gap. Cheapest and probably right: `Report` gains a field naming what
was discarded, and the dispatcher logs it into the attempt's events.jsonl. It
prevents nothing and repairs nothing — it restores attributability, which is
what this whole family actually needs, and it is the same shape as the guard
logging its denials. Anything stronger (rejecting the turn, asking the worker to
resend) reintroduces the failure this fix just removed.

DO NOT resolve this one by making the decoder strict again. That is the bug that
was just closed.
bugs.resolution: 07394d8 (Keel), landed in 6b239be. Report carries discarded: List(String), one line per bugs or posts entry the decoder dropped (for example 'bugs[1]: expected Field at title, found Nothing') and one per field that was not an array; dispatch.write_channels logs a single report_discarded event into the attempt's events.jsonl, with the node and the reasons, only when there is something to confess. The decoder was not made strict again and nothing here can cost a proof outcome; what it restores is attributability, so an attempt with a dropped bug report no longer looks identical to one with nothing to report.

bugs.title: CLAUDE.md forbids switching the shared checkout but never says what it sits on
bugs.body:
Raised by Rowan on 2026-09-06 and left to Keel because closing it means editing
CLAUDE.md, which needs Dib.

WHAT HAPPENED. The shared checkout C:/Users/dibuj/dev/rule30 sat on the feature
branch keel/bug-board all evening, ending up 20 commits behind main. Rowan
fast-forwarded it to main at Dib's direction after verifying the branch was a
strict ancestor. Nothing was lost. The question is why it was possible.

THE GAP, EXACTLY. CLAUDE.md says "The shared checkout has live sessions in it.
Never `git checkout` a different branch there" — a rule about what you must not
DO to that tree. It never says what the tree should be PARKED ON. So a checkout
that drifts onto a feature branch and stays there violates nothing, and the rule
forbidding a checkout is then the very thing that keeps it stuck: nobody may
move it back either.

DIB'S PREFERENCE, stated 2026-09-06: the shared checkout is always on main, and
branch work happens in worktrees.

WHY IT IS MORE THAN TIDINESS. The tree's branch is the default base for anything
started in it, and CLAUDE.md's own worktree section says both of this project's
worktree failures were staleness rather than collision. A shared tree parked on a
feature branch is the same failure with a wider blast radius, because every
session that starts there inherits it silently. It nearly bit twice tonight:
Rowan almost committed a main-destined registry row onto keel/bug-board, and
Fathom flagged that anything running `gleam test` in that tree was testing
harness code without the ports fix or seed.gleam.

FIX: one sentence in CLAUDE.md's "Changing the framework" section saying the
shared checkout is parked on main, alongside the existing rule about not
switching it. NEEDS DIB -- CLAUDE.md is his.

WORTH SAYING PLAINLY: this is a rule that was followed and still produced the
bad state, which is the useful kind of finding. The rule was about the action,
and the hazard was the resting state.
bugs.resolution: Already landed when filed: 441515d (Rowan, 2026-09-06T18:35Z, five minutes after this row) adds to CLAUDE.md "The shared checkout sits on `main`, always" with the fast-forward check for putting it back. Closed by Fathom on a premise check, not a fix.

bugs.title: Two test runners write and delete the same fixture file
bugs.body:
Measured by Fathom on 2026-09-06 against a Keel suite running concurrently.
Filed by Keel, who holds blueprint/bugs.json; Fathom supplied the measurement
and asked for it to be its own entry rather than a paragraph on
`offline-fixtures-write-into-the-live-checkout`. That is the right call and the
reason is the useful part: THAT BUG'S PREMISE IS ONE RUNNER KILLED MID-TEST.
THIS ONE HAPPENS TO TWO RUNNERS THAT ARE BOTH PERFECTLY HEALTHY. Different
premise, different fix, different closure test, so folding them would have made
one entry that is half-fixed forever.

WHAT WAS MEASURED. Fathom's run: `193 passed, 4 failures`, all four at
verify_test.gleam:97 -- `let assert Ok(False) = simplifile.is_file(path)`, the
guard that refuses to start when the fixture file already exists. Going to look
at the leftover found it GONE and the shared checkout clean. A leftover that is
not there afterwards is not a leftover. Keel had reported `195 passed` five
times from another worktree over the same window; both suites were writing and
deleting one file.

THE CAUSE. `probe_id` was a `const`, and `dag.proof_path` derives the file name
from the id, so every runner on this machine resolved the same absolute path.
`HARNESS_REPO_ROOT` does not separate them: both worktrees default it to the
live checkout, because that is the only checkout with a built `.lake`.

CORRECTED 2026-09-06, before anyone acted on it. The entry as first filed said
the destructive direction was "not observed, reachable by inspection". THAT WAS
WRONG, AND KEEL WROTE IT WITHOUT WALKING THE GUARD IT DEPENDS ON. Fathom
analysed the interleavings from the code and Keel confirmed the ordering:
verify_test.gleam:132 checks `is_file` BEFORE the write at :133 and the delete
at :136, and a failed `let assert` panics the test, so a runner that finds a
peer's file aborts and never reaches the delete. Four aborts, zero deletes --
which is exactly what was measured.

So the guard works better than its own docstring claimed: for a killed runner it
turns loss into litter, and for a CONCURRENT runner it turns the destructive
path into a loud abort.

WHAT REMAINS. A narrower window where both runners pass the `is_file` check
before either writes. Both then write, both verify, both delete, and the second
delete fails its own assertion. Every interleaving ends loudly and in
verify_test:

  - `accepts_a_real_proof_test` reading the `sorry` body gets `ContainsSorry`
    and fails `is_verified`.
  - `rejects_sorry_test` reading a valid body gets a verdict that is not
    `ContainsSorry` and fails its `let assert`.
  - `rejects_wrong_statement_test` reading anything else fails its
    `let assert CheckFailed`.
  - A peer's delete landing before `lake build` reads the file gives
    `CheckFailed`, failing whichever test expected otherwise.

NO INTERLEAVING PRODUCES A WRONG VERDICT THAT PASSES. Analysed from the code by
Fathom, not observed, and that is weaker evidence than the collision itself,
which was measured.

WHY THE CORRECTION MATTERS MORE THAN THE ERROR. This board's expensive entries
are the silent ones, and filing a loud bug under a silent-corruption heading
dilutes the category that is doing the work. The severity stays `friction` for
the same reason: it costs a suite run and half an hour chasing a phantom, and
that is what it costs.

THREE READINGS OF ONE FILE AND ONLY THE THIRD IS RIGHT. Rowan saw the file
appear and read it as litter from a killed runner. Keel ruled
`offline-fixtures-write-into-the-live-checkout` stays open on the strength of
the same reading. Fathom looked for the leftover, found it absent, and got the
cause. THE ARTIFACT THAT MISLED TWO OF THREE WAS A DOCSTRING KEEL WROTE
(verify_test.gleam:9-13), which said "a runner killed between the write and the
delete" -- singular, and silent about assuming one. It was not wrong about
anything it said. This is the same family as
`a-discarded-report-field-leaves-no-trace` and
`a-green-suite-can-under-report-and-still-look-green`, and the first instance
where the defective artifact is a comment rather than a record.

FIX, Fathom's suggestion, Keel's commit, in verify_test.gleam only:
`probe_id` becomes `probe_prefix <> "_" <> token()`, where `token/0` is the
existing CSPRNG helper guard.gleam already uses for its auth token -- so nothing
new enters harness_ffi.erl. `harness_probe` takes an id and `verify_with_proof`
builds the node ONCE, since a fresh id per call site would write one file and
verify another. `probe_claims_no_real_node_test` now asserts on the PREFIX: with
a token, any single generated id collides with nothing by luck, so the old form
would have passed without testing anything. `two_fixture_ids_never_collide_test`
fails if `probe_id` ever goes back to being a constant, which nothing else in
the file would catch.

COST, STATED: litter from a killed runner no longer has one known name, so it is
harder to spot and to sweep. Untidy beats silently wrong.

STATUS: fixed on branch keel/report-decoder, sha pending -- nobody is landing
tonight, and this project's convention is that a bug closes against a sha in
main.

OPERATIONAL UNTIL IT LANDS: two sessions cannot both run `gleam test` on this
machine and neither can tell when the other is. Say so before starting.
bugs.resolution: verify_test's fixture id carries a per-run CSPRNG token (`token/0`, the helper guard.gleam already uses for its auth token, so nothing new entered harness_ffi.erl), so no two runners on this machine can name the same file. `harness_probe` takes an id and `verify_with_proof` builds the node once -- a fresh id per call site would write one file and verify another. `probe_claims_no_real_node_test` asserts on the prefix, because with a token any single generated id collides with nothing by luck and the old form would have passed forever without testing anything. `two_fixture_ids_never_collide_test` fails if `probe_id` reverts to a constant. Commit 4931313, in main at 7c80082; 196 passed, fixture cleaned up, checkout clean. Confirmed independently by Rowan, which ran the suite in the shared checkout on the merged tree without announcing it first and did not collide. NOTE: the entry as first filed claimed a destructive direction was reachable. It is not -- corrected in the body before anyone acted on it. POINTER 2026-09-06: Rowan asked for this row's severity to be argued up on the strength of a near-miss where it almost deleted a live fixture during Keel's run. The argument is right and it does not land here -- this row is suite-versus-suite and its fix works. The party that nearly bit is a third one, an overseer tidying untracked files, and what misleads it is that Rule30/Proofs/ is where debris genuinely lives. Recorded on `parked-attempt-leaves-untracked-proof-file`, which was escalated papercut -> friction for it.

bugs.title: dispatch reads guard events by literal substring, so a rename silences the board
bugs.body:
Flagged by Fathom on 2026-09-06 while taking the `Decision` split, and filed
separately at its request rather than folded into that work.

guard.gleam's `event_fields` carries a doc comment saying "dispatch reads these
rows back by literal substring, so these key names are a contract with another
module". The contract is real and it is enforced by `string.contains` over one
module's `string.inspect` output: dispatch.gleam:1104 `denied_tools` matches the
literal `"Deny("`.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THIS BOARD RATHER THAN IN A REFACTOR. The day someone renames
a `Decision` constructor, `denied_tools` returns `[]`, the board silently stops
receiving auto-filed guard bugs, and EVERY TEST STAYS GREEN -- because nothing
asserts that the substring still matches anything. The failure is not that bugs
get filed wrong. It is that the channel goes quiet and quiet is
indistinguishable from a well-behaved fleet.

That is the same shape as `a-discarded-report-field-leaves-no-trace`: an absence
that reads as good news. It is worse than that one in a specific way -- the
report decoder's silent drop needs a worker to have written malformed JSON,
while this one needs only a rename, which is a thing a careful person does on
purpose while cleaning up.

FIX: replace the substring match with a real field. Fathom is doing this as part
of the `Decision` split, which is the right place for it, since the split is
what gives the event a field worth reading. Filed anyway, because a defect
carried inside somebody's in-flight branch is not on the board, and if that
branch is abandoned this goes with it.

NARROWED 2026-09-06 by Keel, NOT CLOSED, on a sweep Fathom asked for rather than
assumed. `guard_denials` (4a4c2e6) replaces the scrape with a decoder, so the
EXTRACTION half is fixed and the forged-field attack it also closed was real --
`attempted` is the one field in that row a worker chooses, and a command
containing the literal text `","denial":"` could have filed itself under a
signature of its choosing.

THE SELECTION HALF IS STILL A SUBSTRING CONTRACT. dispatch.gleam:1117-1118 picks
candidate rows with `string.contains(line, "\"kind\":\"guard\"")` and
`string.contains(line, "\"node\":\"" <> node_id <> "\"")`. Keeping the cheap
filter is deliberate and right -- it is what makes this affordable over thousands
of rows -- but it means the key names `kind` and `node` are still a contract
between two modules enforced by nothing, and renaming either still makes
`guard_denials` select zero rows with every test green. The failure mode this
entry describes is unchanged; only its blast radius shrank.

SWEEP RESULT, so the next person does not redo it. The only other
`string.contains` on another module's output is verify.gleam:110, matching
`harness_check` in Lean's output -- and that is not this shape, because verify
wrote the name it is looking for in the same function. Producer and consumer are
one module. The remaining instance is the dispatch/guard pair above.

CLOSES WHEN the selection uses a decoded field too, or when a test asserts that
the guard's own output still satisfies dispatch's filter -- which would at least
make the contract loud when broken.
bugs.resolution: e859314 and 11acbae (Keel), landed in 6b239be. The guard's log row is one shared type, guard_event.GuardEvent, written by the guard through guard_event.write and read by the dispatcher through guard_event.read, which decodes every line and selects on the decoded kind and node. The two string.contains calls in dispatch.guard_denials and the literal 'guard' in guard.respond_to_hook are gone; log.kind_key names the key the log writes. A rename on either side is a compile error, and a guard that wrote its row any other way fails a test that produces the row over real HTTP and reads it back through dispatch with no test-side spelling of the kind or any key; the negative case was checked by hand and did fail. The denial reason is a typed guard_event.Denial with a Meaning split (Policy or Contention), so counting and auto-filing distinguish a lock timeout from a policy denial. On-disk events.jsonl format unchanged.

bugs.title: #eval false exits 0, so a witness checker on exit status silently passes
bugs.body:
Measured by Keel on 2026-09-06 while designing the falsification witness, and
filed on Fathom's argument that it belongs on the board in its own right rather
than only inside a design ticket.

    $ lake env lean f.lean      # f.lean contains  #eval (false : Bool)
    exit=0   stdout: false

`#eval` on a false Bool is not an error. It is a successful elaboration that
prints `false`. So a witness checker written the obvious way -- run
`lake env lean`, treat exit 0 as a pass -- WOULD PASS EVERY FALSE STATEMENT IT
WAS EVER GIVEN, silently, while reporting that it checked them.

WHY THIS IS `sorry` IN A DIFFERENT COSTUME, which is Fathom's framing and is the
reason it is filed. This project's founding rule is that no agent declares a
proof done by assertion, because `sorry` produces a build that says success. A
witness checker on exit status produces a CHECK that says success. Same failure
mode, one level earlier, and on the statement side where there is no `lake build`
to catch it.

THE RULE THAT FOLLOWS. The verdict must be parsed from stdout, and it needs three
outcomes rather than two, because two of them mean opposite things:

    stdout is exactly `true`   -> holds
    stdout is exactly `false`  -> FALSIFIED, the statement is false on the range
    anything else, or non-zero -> BROKEN CHECK, which is a bug in the witness and
                                  says nothing about the statement

Collapsing the last two is the defect this entry exists to prevent: a witness
that fails to elaborate is not evidence that the statement is false.

AND A FOURTH, FROM THE MEASUREMENT ON `seeding-has-no-verifier-and-no-role`: a
timeout is `unchecked`, never a pass. `List.all` short-circuits, so a false
witness returns instantly and a true one pays the full 3^t -- which means A
TIMEOUT CORRELATES WITH THE STATEMENT BEING TRUE, and a checker that read
"no falsification found before the deadline" as success would pass exactly the
statements too expensive to check. Fathom's corollary, worth keeping: the timeout
budget cannot be tuned by watching how long checks take, because the ones that
time out are systematically the ones you most wanted an answer to.
bugs.resolution: Already fixed when filed. seed.witness_verdict (684fa35, hardened in 732d744, both twelve minutes before this row) reads the text lake env lean printed: WitnessHolds only for exactly 'true' at exit 0, Falsified for exactly 'false', WitnessBroken for anything else or a non-zero exit, Unchecked for a timeout. seed_test pins each arm, including a live-toolchain calibration. Two gaps found beside it and closed in 656667c (Keel), landed in 6b239be: a route of 'sorry' elaborates with exit 0 and only a warning (measured: 'warning: declaration uses sorry'), so check_route now returns RouteUsesSorry when a zero exit carries that warning, pinned by a live test; and a placeholder witness such as the literal 'true' passes any checker, so check_witness now refuses, before Lean runs, an expression that mentions no whole-token identifier from the statement it witnesses (WitnessPlaceholder, its own count and wording). What it deliberately does not catch, and says so: a witness that names the right definition and evaluates something unrelated.

bugs.title: One bad row in bugs.json turns off auto-filing for the rest of the run
bugs.body:
Hit by Rowan on 2026-09-06 by hand-writing an entry, traced by Fathom, and
verified independently by Keel at the call sites before filing, because it is
being filed as `blocks`.

WHAT HAPPENS. bugs.gleam:430 is `decode.list(bug_decoder())`, so ONE malformed
row fails the WHOLE board decode. Rowan appended an entry with the six fields
that were visible in the rows it sampled; the decoder named nine it had omitted
and the entire file failed to render.

THE CONSEQUENCE IS NOT "THE BOARD WILL NOT RENDER". Both callers --
dispatch.gleam:1004 and :1057 -- handle the failure as
`Error(reason) -> io.println_error(...)`. So a decode failure means THE
DISPATCHER FILES NOTHING, for every remaining attempt in the run, and says so
only on stderr. That line does not reach the attempt's events.jsonl, so the run
record shows a normal run that happened to file no bugs -- WHICH IS EXACTLY WHAT
A CLEAN RUN LOOKS LIKE. The failure mode is a success report. Same family as
`a-discarded-report-field-leaves-no-trace` and
`a-green-suite-can-under-report-and-still-look-green`.

WHAT IS NOT WRONG, checked specifically because it would have been catastrophic:
nothing does `bugs.load |> result.unwrap(Board([]))` before a `save`. `save`
re-encodes from what was loaded, so that combination would have WIPED the board.
Both `save` calls (dispatch.gleam:1033, :1082) sit inside their load's `Ok` arm.
That is not luck, it is the `Error` arms doing their job.

SECOND HALF, Rowan's, and the one that costs time: `UnableToDecode` named nine
missing FIELDS and not which of the 29 ENTRIES was wrong. On a board this size
that is a bisect by hand.

THE OBVIOUS FIX IS WRONG HERE, and this is the part worth reading. The instinct
is to copy 3b4b867 -- `decode.list(decode.dynamic)` plus `list.filter_map`, so a
bad element is dropped. That is right for a WORKER REPORT, where the promise is
that nothing a worker adds may cost the proof outcome, so dropping is the safe
direction. IT IS WRONG FOR THE BOARD. A dropped row is a filed bug, and because
`save` rewrites the whole file from what was loaded, A SILENT DROP AT LOAD
BECOMES A PERMANENT DELETION AT THE NEXT SAVE. Fathom's catch.

SO: decode each element independently to FIND the bad one, then STILL FAIL --
naming the index and the `id` if it has one. Loud and located, not lenient. And
route the load failure into the attempt's events.jsonl so the run record says
filing was off, rather than looking clean.

THE SAMPLING ERROR UNDERNEATH IT, Rowan's, and it is a new variant: the entry was
well-formed JSON, it round-tripped, and its fields were ones Rowan had seen with
its own eyes in the file. THE SCHEMA IS WIDER THAN ANY SINGLE ENTRY DISPLAYS,
because the optional-looking fields are absent from the rows it sampled. Reading
the file teaches you a subset and gives no signal that it is one.
bugs.resolution: bugs.decode now tries the strict decoder, and on failure re-parses the board as untyped rows and runs bug_decoder against each independently to say WHICH rows are bad, by index and by id -- then still returns Error. Loud and located, not lenient, for the reason in the body: a dropped board row is a filed bug and `save` rewrites from what it loaded, so a silent drop at load is a permanent deletion at the next save. Both dispatch.gleam load-failure arms now call `filing_disabled`, which keeps the stderr line and adds a `filing_disabled` event to the attempt's own log, so the run record says the channel was off rather than looking like a clean run that filed nothing. Commit 2470707, verified an ancestor of origin/main before citation. THREE THINGS FATHOM RECORDED AGAINST ITSELF WHILE FIXING IT, kept because they are the useful part. The third decode branch: if the text is not a {bugs: [...]} object at all there are no rows to blame, so the original parse error is returned unchanged -- a fault list asserting zero malformed entries while refusing the board would be its own small well-formed-and-wrong. The mutation: Fathom predicted one test would die and six did, three of them because the reason it gave for their surviving was the reason they die. And the redundancy: two of the six, `unknown_area_fails_the_decode_test` and `unknown_status_fails_the_decode_test`, already pinned the strictness -- they date from eff5fc9, written by Keel, who had forgotten them and then agreed with Fathom that the property needed pinning. Neither read the file they were both reasoning about. The new test is kept as a documented duplicate because it states the REASON where the older two state the property.

bugs.title: A claimed node names an identity, not an address anyone can test for liveness
bugs.body:
Rowan's finding, Fathom's framing, filed by Keel.

A `claimed` node records an `identity` and a `session_id`. `ListAgents` -- the
only thing that authoritatively knows who is alive, from outside the process and
without its cooperation -- answers in refs like `de0407`. THE TWO DO NOT JOIN. So
nothing can tell a live claim from one held by a session that died an hour ago,
and `reopen` stays a human judgement call about a fact a machine could establish.

THIS IS A MISSING JOIN KEY, NOT A MISSING FEATURE. Rowan's phrase and it is the
right one: the liveness information exists and the claim record exists, and there
is no column connecting them. `agents/sessions.json` maps ref to identity, but a
session that never registers is invisible to it -- which happened three times on
2026-09-06 alone, including to Keel.

`/startup`'s `state.sh` reports claimed rows and SAYS OUT LOUD that it cannot
cross-reference them. That is the right behaviour and it is not a fix: it makes
the gap visible without making it checkable, which is strictly better than
implying a cross-reference it cannot perform.

DELIBERATELY SEPARATE from `a-held-claim-has-an-owner-but-no-expiry`. A lease
makes an abandoned claim self-evident without anyone asking who held it; this
entry is about being able to ask. Fixing either leaves the other standing.

A THIRD INSTANCE, observed 2026-09-06 by Fathom, and it is the same shape in a
place nobody had named. `verify_test`'s fixture now carries a per-run token
(4931313), so two runners no longer collide and a leftover file is identifiable
as SOME runner's rather than as anonymous debris. It still does not say WHICH
runner. So a genuinely abandoned fixture remains unattributable, and the
question "whose is this" is now unanswered by design in three places: a claimed
node, a held lock, and a leftover file.

That is not a criticism of the fixture fix, which solved the collision it was
aimed at. It is that IDENTIFIABLE AND ATTRIBUTABLE ARE DIFFERENT PROPERTIES, and
tokens buy the first while only a join key buys the second. Worth having in this
entry because the fixture case is the one where the gap is cheapest to see.

Live demonstration on the same day, both directions. Fathom saw a token-bearing
fixture in the shared checkout and did NOT report it as litter -- correctly, it
was Keel's suite mid-run -- where earlier the same evening both Rowan and Fathom
had reported an untokenised one as litter and both were wrong. The token made the
file legible enough to prompt the right question. Answering it still took asking
a human.

BOARD HALF (Fathom, 2026-09-07, 2191f23). `bugs claim <id> --as <You>
--session <ref>` stores the holder's ListAgents ref as `claimed_ref`, and
state.sh prints it as `[ref ...]` beside the claim, so the join this row
asks for exists for a bug: read the ref off the report, find it in
ListAgents, done. It is optional, because a session learns its ref only by
calling ListAgents and a claim should not be refused for the lack of it; the
take-bug skill tells every claimant to pass it.

THE DAG HALF STAYS OPEN. A node claim records `session_id`, the Claude
session UUID, and ListAgents answers in six-character refs; the two still do
not join, and the dispatcher is the only thing that could write the ref at
claim time. That is a dispatch.gleam change and belongs to whoever is in
that file.

The fixture case is unchanged: a leftover verify_test fixture is
identifiable as some runner's and attributable to none.
bugs.resolution: 6be520c (Keel), landed in 3aa8d97; the board half was Fathom's --session ref on bugs claim, this is the DAG half. A claimed node now records claimed_by, claimed_at and claimed_run, set by dag.claim at both dispatch sites (prove-one and the run loop) and cleared by dag.release on every exit from Claimed: attempt returned, attempt crashed, hand reopen. A dispatched prover is not a registered session, so the checkable reference is the run id: runs/<run>/summary.txt exists exactly once that run has ended, and status, reopen and the prove-one refusal print holder, age, run id and that ended-or-not fact through one claim_text. The check is one-sided by construction and says so: an absent summary cannot tell a live run from one that died, and then the age is the only clue. Older dag.json rows decode with the fields absent. Suite 364/364 on the merged tree.

bugs.title: A claim records who holds it but not when, so abandoned looks like busy
bugs.body:
Rowan's finding, filed by Keel, and the cheaper of the pair with
`a-claim-does-not-name-a-session-anyone-can-check`.

A lock with an owner is indistinguishable from a lock held by someone still
thinking. A LEASE WITH A TIMESTAMP IS SELF-EVIDENTLY ABANDONED. That difference
needs no liveness lookup, no join key and no cooperation from the holder, which
is why it is the cheaper fix and why it should probably land first.

IT IS ALSO THE ONLY ONE OF THE PAIR THAT COVERS A PROMISE LIVING SOLELY IN A PEER
MESSAGE. On 2026-09-06 the build lock was hand-passed between three sessions all
evening entirely in messages -- "taking it", "clear now" -- and appears in no
file. Nothing but the participants' memory recorded who held it. A session that
died mid-hold would have left the other two waiting on a promise with no
artifact. That is precisely the case CLAUDE.md's rule is about: state that must
survive a session dying without warning has to be derivable from outside the
process, or be inert when stale. A lease is the "inert when stale" half.

WHY BOTH ENTRIES AND NOT ONE. Even with leases, WHO held this and IS THAT SESSION
ALIVE stay unlinkable, and that is what bites a human reading the report at 2am.
Fathom's argument for the split, and it is right.

BOTH HALVES READABLE (Fathom, 2026-09-07, bb52b40 and 2191f23). A bug claim
made through `bugs claim` carries `claimed_at`, and state.sh prints its age.
It was worse than the title says: a hand-claimed row carried no holder
either, so "an owner but no expiry" was "neither" on the board.

A DAG node claim still has no timestamp field, and it turned out the node's
own record cannot supply one: an attempt row is appended when the attempt
ENDS, so every node claimed by a live run has no row and looked exactly like
one whose dispatcher died before writing -- three of them did, during run
20260907T015318Z, on the first version of this fix. The dispatch event in
runs/ is written when the attempt starts and is the only timestamp a node
claim has; state.sh now reads the latest one for the node and prints who it
went to, when, and how long ago. That is the lease this row asked for, read
from outside the process rather than stored on the claim, which is the
CLAUDE.md rule for state that must survive a session dying. No dispatch.gleam
change was needed for it.

The promise-in-a-peer-message case is not fixable by a field. What landed
for it is the rule: a promise names the wall-clock moment it lapses
(`a-stated-default-without-a-clock-time-is-a-countdown`).
bugs.resolution: bb52b40 and 2191f23 (Fathom): a bug claim carries claimed_at and state.sh prints its age; a node claim is dated from its dispatch event in runs/, read by state.sh, because the node's own attempt row is only written when the attempt ends. Both leases are readable without the holder. The promise-in-a-message case has no field and got a rule instead, a-stated-default-without-a-clock-time-is-a-countdown.

bugs.title: two agents agreeing on a premise neither looked up reads as review and is not
bugs.body:
Filed by Rowan on 2026-09-06. The finding is Keel's and Fathom's as much as mine; Keel asked that it go in my words and supplied the correction that makes it accurate.

WHAT HAPPENED, TWICE. Fathom landed six tests and predicted one would die under mutation. Six died. Two of those died redundantly, because the property they claimed to pin was already pinned by tests from eff5fc9 — Keel's own commit. So the strictness was already guarded by the person who then agreed with Fathom that it needed guarding. Earlier the same evening, Fathom measured guard denials as 21/12/9; Keel re-ran it and got 25 over 23 events, 15/9/1. In both cases two agents discussed a premise at length and neither looked it up.

WHAT THIS IS NOT. It is not a failure to review. The review was good and it was mutual: Fathom caught Keel's unwalked run directory, Keel caught Fathom's over-broad classifier, I caught a board entry whose lead taught the wrong test. Every one of those is a peer catching a peer's REASONING.

WHAT IT IS. What went unchecked both times was a PREMISE neither party had looked up — what the tests already covered, what the log files actually contained. Reviewing an argument cannot catch a false premise, because a valid argument from a false premise reads as correct to everyone in the conversation, and a second agent agreeing raises confidence without adding evidence. Agreement is the cheapest thing two agents can produce and it is indistinguishable, from outside, from verification.

WHERE THE EVIDENCE ACTUALLY CAME FROM. A mutation run and a `git log`. Not from either agent, and not from the exchange between them. That is the diagnostic: if the thing that settled a question was a command, the discussion before it was not what checked it.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THIS BOARD. `a-bugs-premise-is-never-checked-before-it-is-fixed` already names this class for bugs. This is the same rule escaping the board and applying to the agents: we built a premise check for entries and then reasoned to each other without one. The project has exactly one adjudicator, `lake build`, and it only ever looks at proofs — so everything framework agents say to each other reads identically whether it is true or false, and agreement between two of us adds no adjudication at all.

POSSIBLE SHAPES OF A FIX, none obviously right. A convention that a claim about the repo carries the command that produced it, so a peer can re-run rather than agree. A habit of stating which premise a conclusion rests on, so the thing to look up is named. Or accepting that this is not fixable by protocol and belongs in CLAUDE.md as a known hazard, which is a legitimate answer and should be recorded as one rather than left open indefinitely.

--- AMENDED by Rowan, 2026-09-06T22:30Z: the positive case ---

Three times on 2026-09-06 a review between Rowan and Keel was agreement, and the tie was broken by something other than the review. Twice it was a tool (a mutant, a count). The third was not a tool: after run 20260906T210938Z had been reviewed, verified and landed, Rowan re-read the last node's proof note and found it claimed P1 was proved; later, re-reading a brief already landed, Rowan found a hardcoded count that had gone false within the hour. Both times what worked was going back to the artifact, not re-arguing the argument.

The rule that follows, in Keel's words: review that returns to the artifact catches what review of the argument cannot. It is the only version of peer review that has actually worked here, and it is cheap: read the file, not the message about the file.

TAKE-BUG SKILL (Fathom, 2026-09-07, e596660). The first shape of fix the body
offers -- a claim about the repo carries the command that produced it, so a
peer re-runs rather than agrees -- is now a step in
.claude/skills/take-bug/SKILL.md: the command is the check, the paste is the
record, and "if what settled the question was a conversation rather than a
command, it is not settled" is in its text. Rowan's amendment (return to the
artifact, not the argument) is its shape-B rule.

The third shape the body offers, recording this as a known hazard in
CLAUDE.md, is the one that would close the row and it needs Dib. Left open
for that decision.
bugs.resolution: Closed on a premise check by Keel, 2026-09-07, for the bug-work path: e596660 (Fathom) take-bug skill, section 2, states that if what settled a question was a conversation with a peer rather than a command, the question is not settled, and its red-flag table names 'a peer confirmed it' as the thought to distrust; Rowan's amendment (return to the artifact, quote by git show or file:line) is the same section's shape-B rule. What remains is outside any bug claim: a premise asserted in a peer message and agreed to is still unadjudicated, and the row's own third shape, recording this as a known hazard in CLAUDE.md, has not happened because CLAUDE.md needs Dib; Rowan carries that paragraph to him with the other CLAUDE.md items. The row closes rather than carrying a landed fix indefinitely.

bugs.title: blueprint/bugs.json is one line, so any two edits conflict and the obvious fix drops a row
bugs.body:
Filed by Rowan on 2026-09-06, after hitting it. I had told Keel I would not file this, on the grounds that I had already written to this file twice tonight and both times something went wrong. That is squeamishness rather than judgment, and it is the red flag my own /checkpoint skill lists.

WHAT HAPPENED. Cherry-picking Keel's e4f6b02 onto main conflicted on this file. Keel's commit was based on a version without the row I had filed as 0dd975e a few minutes earlier, so git had two edits and no way to combine them.

WHY IT WILL HAPPEN EVERY TIME. blueprint/bugs.json is a single line of JSON. Git merges line by line, so ANY two edits to the board touch the same line and conflict, no matter how far apart the rows are or how unrelated the changes. This is not a race that concurrency makes likely; it is guaranteed whenever two branches both add a row, which is the normal case with two framework agents.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY CONFLICT. A conflict here shows as one changed line containing the entire board, so the diff a human reviews is unreadable and offers no guidance about what to keep. The obvious resolution — take one side — silently drops the other agent's row, and nothing downstream notices: the file still parses, the decoder still succeeds, the board still renders, and the missing finding looks exactly like a finding nobody filed. That is this project's characteristic failure shape, and this is a path straight into it.

HOW I RESOLVED IT, since it is the safe recipe and not obvious. Take the incoming version of the file whole, then recover your own row VERBATIM out of git (`git show <sha>:blueprint/bugs.json`, parse, pull the row by id) and splice it in. Never retype a row during a resolution. Then verify before continuing: ids unique, expected count, and `gleam run -- bugs --all` renders through the real decoder.

POSSIBLE FIXES, in rough order of cost. Pretty-print the file one field per line, so git can merge non-adjacent rows and a conflict is legible — costs one large reformat commit and makes the file's diffs readable forever after. Or give the harness a filing command (`gleam run -- file-bug`), which also fixes `a-malformed-board-row-silently-disables-auto-filing`, since nobody would hand-write the sixteen fields. Or split the board into one file per bug, which removes the conflict entirely and costs a directory. Doing nothing is defensible if the recipe above is written down somewhere an agent will find it, but right now it exists only in this entry.

FOURTH STEP, added by Keel after hitting this and nearly losing a row to the
recipe itself. The recipe as written says: take the incoming file whole, recover
your own row VERBATIM out of `git show <sha>:blueprint/bugs.json`, splice, then
check ids and count and render. That is right and it is incomplete.

IT RECOVERS ROWS YOU EDITED AND SILENTLY DROPS ROWS YOU ADDED. Iterating the
incoming board and substituting your version of the entries you changed never
visits an entry the incoming board does not have. On 2026-09-06 that lost
`a-stated-default-without-a-clock-time-is-a-countdown` — a row filed forty
minutes earlier, in the same working tree, by the same agent doing the merge. No
conflict, no warning, and a row count that looked plausible because the incoming
board had grown by three in the meantime.

SO THE RESOLUTION IS TWO SETS, NOT ONE:
  rows you EDITED  -> yours wins, verbatim from the sha
  rows only YOU have -> appended, verbatim from the sha
and the check afterwards is not "does it render" but "is every id from BOTH
parents present in the result". Two explicit difference lists, printed and read.

WHAT ACTUALLY CAUGHT IT was not care. It was having written the expected ids out
by hand beforehand so the verification printed one line per row with True or
False on it, and one of them said False. A count would not have caught it; a
render would not have caught it; `ids unique` would not have caught it. The only
check that could return "no" here was the one that named, in advance, what had to
be there.

THE RECIPE WAS WRONG AT ITS PREMISE, found by Keel using it on 2026-09-06 and
nearly losing a row to it a second time in a different way.

Both the four-step recipe and the fifth step added above compare TWO versions:
mine and the incoming. That conflates two different things — I CHANGED THIS ROW
and THEY CHANGED THIS ROW AFTER MY SNAPSHOT — because both present as
`mine != theirs`. Taking "mine" for the second case reverts their change
silently, with no conflict and no count moving.

It fired on `guard-denied-bash-not-permitted-2`, which Keel never edited at all.
The dispatcher had bumped `occurrences` 2 -> 3 and updated `filed` during the
run. A two-way merge classified it as a row Keel had edited and would have put
back the stale copy, discarding a recorded denial.

AND THE FIFTH STEP DID NOT CATCH IT, because the fifth step diffs BODIES and the
loss was in `occurrences` and `filed`. A row whose body is identical can still
have lost everything that made it worth re-reading.

THE FIX IS A THREE-WAY MERGE, against the commit your snapshot was taken from:

    mine != base, theirs == base   -> I changed it. Take mine.
    mine == base, theirs != base   -> THEY changed it. Take theirs.
    both != base                   -> a real conflict. Take my body, and take
                                      THEIR dispatcher-owned fields
                                      (`occurrences`, `filed`, `status`,
                                      `resolution`, `fixed`), because those are
                                      written by the running harness and my
                                      snapshot of them is only stale.
    in one parent only             -> keep it.

Then the checks: every id from both parents present, ids unique, and for any row
in the both-changed case, every paragraph of theirs present in the result.

WHY THIS KEPT GOING WRONG. Each version of the recipe answered a question one
step weaker than the one it was being asked. "Is the row there" is weaker than
"did my edit survive", which is weaker than "did THEIR edit survive", which is
weaker than "did their edit to a field I never looked at survive". The base is
what makes the question answerable at all — without it, staleness and
authorship are the same observation.
bugs.resolution: 2191f23 (Fathom): the encoder writes one bug per line, so rows that do not touch merge cleanly and a real conflict is one legible row. The three-way recipe in this body still applies to a conflict on the same row, and the dispatcher-owned fields still win there. Every board write should now go through the harness (bugs claim, reopen, close, or the dispatcher); a hand edit that reformats the file makes the next diff unreadable once.

bugs.title: A haiku failure on a hard node is scored as if it were about the node
bugs.body:
Filed by Rowan after re-evaluating direction with Dib on 2026-09-06. Dib's ruling, verbatim in spirit: a haiku first try should not count for much as a failure.

WHAT THE LADDER DOES. config.ladder is by size, cheapest first: S runs haiku, sonnet, opus; M skips haiku; L goes straight to opus. That is the right shape and this ticket does not ask to change it. What it asks about is what a failure on the bottom rung MEANS afterwards.

THE DEFECT. Every failed attempt is one more entry in the node's attempts, and three readers treat that count as evidence about the node: the ladder (failed_attempts picks the next model), the size calibration in roster.gleam, and the overseer reading the board. A haiku attempt that dies budget_exhausted on a node whose real proof is one line (bool_map_iterate_three, 41 turns, $0.38) is evidence about haiku and about the description, not about the node, and today it is recorded identically to an opus attempt that fails after real search.

This is the sibling of harness-caused-abandonment-is-scored-as-difficulty, which is about attempts the HARNESS broke. This one is about attempts that were never a fair test: the model was below the node. Both corrupt the same signal in the same direction.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT. Weight an attempt's evidential value by its rung, or simply exclude bottom-rung failures from calibration and from any difficulty reading the overseer is offered. Cheapest version: the status output and the run summary say which rung each failed attempt was on, so a reader can discount it by eye; the calibration code excludes attempts whose model is below the node's ladder top. A haiku failure should cost one rung and nothing else.

WHY IT MATTERS NOW. Direction is moving toward research nodes near P1 (see the spine tier seeded 2026-09-06). Those nodes will collect failures by design, and every one of them will look like difficulty unless the record says which failures were probes.
bugs.resolution: 6d3c0a0 and 3759943 (Keel), landed in 6b239be. roster.tally scores calibration for an attempt that closed the node at any rung or was made on the top rung of its ladder (the last entry of config.ladder(node.size)), and never for one the harness broke; so a haiku that died on an S node costs its rung and moves no calibration figure, while a haiku that closed one counts exactly as an opus close would. A Wall, having no ladder, contributes no failed-attempt evidence. The status row appends the models of failed and harness-broken attempts (attempts=4 failed=haiku,sonnet harness=opus) so a reader can see which attempts were probes. The ladder's shape was not changed.

bugs.title: A research node gets one 40-turn opus attempt and is then marked exhausted
bugs.body:
Filed by Rowan after re-evaluating direction with Dib on 2026-09-06.

WHAT HAPPENS TODAY. config.model_for drops one ladder entry per failed attempt and returns Error when the list is empty, so every rung gets exactly one attempt. The budget is global: HARNESS_MAX_TURNS 40 and HARNESS_MAX_BUDGET_USD 4.0 regardless of size or rung. An L node therefore gets one opus attempt of at most 40 turns and is then abandoned as ladder exhausted. Fable is not on any ladder.

WHY THAT IS WRONG FOR THE DIRECTION THE PROJECT IS NOW TAKING. For the edge lemmas the ladder was a cost optimiser and it was right. For a node where nobody knows the proof, one 40-turn attempt is a probe, not a search, and abandoning after it throws away the only thing such a node can produce: partial structure and candidate sub-lemmas (see a-worker-report-has-no-sub-lemma-section). Dib's stated goal is to maximise the chance, however small, of an actual solution, and the top of the ladder is the only place that chance lives.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT. Keep the ladder as it is below the top. At the top rung, for a node marked research (a new size or a flag; Wall is close but means never dispatch), allow repeated attempts on the same rung, from different provers with different notebooks, with a per-rung turn and dollar budget rather than the global one. A research node is never ladder-exhausted; it is dispatched when a slot is free and nothing cheaper is startable. Add Fable as the top rung. The one-session-per-persona rule already makes diversity natural: the second attempt on a research node goes to a different persona in the region.

NOT ASKING FOR TONIGHT. This is a direction change to dispatch.gleam and config.gleam and it waits for a framework agent with the board quiet.
bugs.resolution: 4fdba16 and e0778e1 (Keel), landed in dfa9f4a, Rowan's proposed shape as Dib approved it. A captain-set research: true on a dag.json node (encoded only when true, like object) makes its top rung repeatable: config.model_for never exhausts such a node, record never abandons it, and after the ladder's cheap rungs are spent one attempt each, every further attempt runs at the top rung under HARNESS_RESEARCH_MAX_TURNS (120) and HARNESS_RESEARCH_MAX_BUDGET_USD (20.0) instead of the global 40 and 4.0; the dispatch event records the budget and the brief tells the worker its ceilings. Fable is the top rung of every ladder now, so an ordinary node gains one rung before abandonment. The scheduler offers a research leaf only behind every ordinary open leaf. One premise corrected: the one-session-per-persona rule alone did not give diversity at concurrency one, since the first persona is idle again when the second attempt starts, so at a research node's top rung the chooser prefers an idle persona that has not tried the node, minting only when the region's rule already would. Calibration counts the top two rungs so evidence gathered before fable was added still counts. status marks such nodes research. Suite 466/466 on the merged tree.

bugs.title: A failed attempt on a hard node produces nothing the DAG can use
bugs.body:
Filed by Rowan after re-evaluating direction with Dib on 2026-09-06.

THE GAP. A worker either closes its node or fails, and a failure produces an attempt row, a notebook entry and a journal entry. None of those is a statement. A person attacking a hard theorem decomposes it into lemmas; the harness gives a worker no channel to hand a decomposition back, so a hard node only ever escalates the ladder and the DAG never grows from an attempt. Every node on the board today was typed by the captain, which is the supply problem that emptied the board twice on 2026-09-06.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT. Add a proposed-sub-lemmas section to the structured end-of-turn report: each proposal is a Lean statement (exactly as it would be seeded, with a name), one sentence on why it would help close the node, and a size estimate. The dispatcher writes them to the attempt directory as a proposal file in the shape Keel's seeder check consumes (see seeding-has-no-verifier-and-no-role and the seeder spec), so a worker's proposals go through the same statement check and the same review-and-land step as a seeder's. Rowan reviews and lands; a worker never writes Statements.lean or dag.json, same as a seeder.

Two guards worth building in from the start. A proposal is not a claim the node is hard: a haiku attempt may propose freely and its proposals are weighed by the check, not by the rung. And a proposal that restates the node under another name, or weakens it, is the failure the type_of% check exists for on the proof side and needs the same treatment here.

WHY IT MATTERS. This is the mechanism that turns the top of the ladder (see the-top-rung-gets-one-attempt-then-abandons) from a cost into a source of DAG growth. Without it, repeated attempts on a research node are repeated probes with no memory but the notebook.

bugs.title: "Otherwise I proceed" is an announcement wearing a question's clothes
bugs.body:
Rowan's phrasing, Keel's generalisation, filed by Keel. Observed on 2026-09-06
between two live framework sessions, and demonstrated a second time in the act of
filing it.

WHAT HAPPENED. Rowan found a defect in Keel's commit, said "tell me and I will
hold the landing; otherwise I land as-is", and landed inside the same working
stretch -- never pausing at a point where a reply could arrive. Cost nothing:
the follow-up fix fast-forwarded cleanly. Had Keel wanted the fix folded into the
original commit, the push had already made that impossible, and Keel would have
learned it from the result rather than from Rowan.

THE DEFECT, IN ROWAN'S WORDS: a question with a stated default, acted on before
the reply can arrive, is a COUNTDOWN -- and the peer cannot beat a countdown that
expires inside one tool call.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A BARE ANNOUNCEMENT rather than more polite than one. The
reply window is bounded by the sender's own next action, and the sender is the
only party who can see how long that is. So the recipient cannot measure the
deadline it is being held to, and cannot tell a real invitation from a formality.
A bare "I am landing this" at least does not imply a say the recipient never had.
Every framework session on 2026-09-06 wrote this construction; Keel wrote it at
least three times.

AND IT IS UNCHECKABLE BY THE SENDER TOO, which is what makes it structural rather
than a lapse. Rowan: "a deadline the setter has not yet measured cannot be checked
by anyone, including the setter" -- the length of that working stretch was not
decided until Rowan was inside it. There is no moment at which looking harder
would have helped. Contrast the same day's other error, Keel reading a "replaced
4" it had not predicted: that was a value available to be checked and not checked,
which a habit fixes. This one needs a structural stop.

THE FIX IS NOT "DO NOT STATE A DEFAULT". A default is genuinely better than an
open question when the peer may be dead -- that is the whole lesson of
`a-held-claim-has-an-owner-but-no-expiry`, and of Fathom's clean exit, where a
statement made while alive about what would be true afterwards is what made its
silence safe to read.

THE FIX IS THAT THE DEFAULT MUST NAME THE WALL-CLOCK MOMENT IT FIRES.
"I land at 20:45Z unless you say otherwise" is answerable. "Otherwise I land
as-is" is not. Same repair as the lease, applied to an intention instead of to a
claim: a promise whose expiry only one party can see is not a promise the other
party can act on.

FILED ONE LIVE COLLISION LATER, WHICH IS THE EVIDENCE. Keel announced it was
taking blueprint/bugs.json before touching the file; Rowan was three minutes from
filing the same row and stopped. Nothing enforced that -- there is no lock on the
board, and per `the-board-is-one-line-so-two-editors-always-conflict` two
concurrent edits always conflict. It worked only because the claim was announced
BEFORE the write rather than after it. Announcing on completion is the courteous
habit and it would have produced a merge conflict on the board, about a row on the
value of announcing early.
bugs.resolution: bb52b40 (Fathom): the rule lives where the sentence gets written. The checkpoint skill says the expiry must be a clock time, not a condition, with the countdown as a red flag; the startup skill's speak-first paragraph says to know whether you are announcing or asking, and to name the wall-clock moment a default fires. Nothing enforces it; nothing could.

bugs.title: A worker's English can claim a prize the Lean does not prove
bugs.body:
Observed by Rowan on 2026-09-06 in run 20260906T210938Z, on the last node of the
P1 spine. Filed by Keel.

WHAT HAPPENED. The worker wrote a `/-!` proof note and a journal entry claiming
P1 was proved. **The Lean was exactly the conditional statement that was seeded,
and the harness checked its type.** Only the English overclaimed. Rowan rewrote
the note and appended a correction to the run journal.

WHY THIS IS THE MOST DANGEROUS INSTANCE OF THE FAMILY THIS BOARD KEEPS FINDING.
Every other entry is a record that misleads an agent. This one misleads THE
PROJECT OWNER ABOUT WHETHER A PRIZE CONJECTURE WAS PROVED. The verifier did its
job perfectly: `type_of%` pinned the theorem to the seeded statement, the axioms
were clean, `lake build` was green. Everything the harness adjudicates was
correct. The claim that was false was in the one artifact the harness reads and
never checks — and it is the artifact a human actually reads, because CLAUDE.md
says the note exists precisely so Dib does not have to read the tactic script.

SO THE PROJECT'S FOUNDING GUARANTEE HAS A SEAM IN IT. "No agent declares a proof
done by assertion" is true of the THEOREM and false of the PROSE ABOUT the
theorem. `verify.gleam` adjudicates a type; nothing adjudicates a sentence. And
the note is written by the same session, in the same turn, as the proof it
describes — so a worker that has misunderstood what it proved will write a note
that is wrong in exactly the way its misunderstanding was, confidently, and
nothing downstream can tell.

NOT A WORKER FAILURE, AND THE FIX IS NOT "TELL WORKERS TO BE CAREFUL". A
conditional theorem whose hypothesis is the hard part genuinely looks like the
thing it is conditional on, especially to a session that has just spent twenty
turns inside it. The three-heading note format asks for "what this says" in one
sentence with no Lean in it, which is exactly the pressure that turns
`h -> P1` into "P1".

CANDIDATE FIXES, none chosen.
  - A seeded statement carries, IN THE CAPTAIN'S VOICE, what it does NOT prove,
    and the brief hands that to the worker as the thing its note must not
    contradict. Rowan's proposal, and the cheapest — it puts the disclaimer
    where a human wrote it rather than asking the worker to derive it.
  - The prize files are `sorry` forever and the harness knows their names.
    Anything asserting a prize name is proved, in a note or a journal, could at
    least be flagged for a human — cheap, mechanical, and catches this exact
    case.
  - Nothing that asks the worker to self-assess. A note is a worker's account of
    its own turn, and the failure here is that the account was sincere.

RELATED: `a-verified-route-can-be-verified-against-the-wrong-object` is the same
shape one step earlier — something was checked, but not the thing that shipped.
The difference is that a bad route costs a rung and a bad note costs the
project's ability to know what it has.

TWO FAILURES, TWO SHAPES — Rowan, on re-reading the same worker's output, and
this halves the value of the fix that was already built.

  1. THE OVERCLAIM. The `/-!` note turned `h -> P1` into "P1". Format pressure:
     the note format asks for one Lean-free sentence saying what the theorem
     says, and a conditional whose hypothesis is the whole difficulty comes out
     of that squeeze as the unconditional claim. `disclaims` addresses this,
     because a captain writing the boundary in advance is exactly what the
     worker was being asked to derive.

  2. THE CONFABULATED MECHANISM, WHICH `disclaims` DOES NOT TOUCH. The same
     worker's journal says the proof works by "the entire left side of the
     cone, all diagonals, collapsing via the propagation lemmas". THE DIAGONALS
     PLAY NO PART IN THE SPINE. That is not a squeezed sentence; it is a model
     narrating a chain it imagined after finishing a different one. No
     disclaimer a captain writes anticipates a mechanism the worker invents,
     because the captain cannot enumerate the things that are not true.

WHY THAT MATTERS BEYOND THIS BUG. A note that overclaims is wrong about scope
and can be bounded in advance. A note that confabulates a mechanism is wrong
about WHAT HAPPENED, is internally coherent, cites real lemmas from the
project, and reads exactly like an explanation. Only a reader who knows the
proof catches it — which is the one resource this harness is built to spend
less of.

RANKING CHANGED, Rowan's, and Keel agrees. The mechanical prize-name flag now
ranks ABOVE `disclaims` rather than beside it: both of tonight's instances said
"P1" in so many words, so a check that flags any note or journal asserting a
prize name is proved would have caught BOTH — the bounded failure and the
unbounded one. `disclaims` catches only the first, and only when a captain
anticipated it.

`disclaims` shipped in 4c9dd85 and is worth having. It does not close this row,
and it now demonstrably addresses one of the two shapes rather than the defect.

THE DECISION, WRITTEN DOWN RATHER THAN LEFT IN MESSAGES, because that is the
failure this board spent 2026-09-06 repairing. Rowan is putting it to Dib; the
options and the reasoning are here so the decision is made against a record
rather than against whoever remembers the conversation.

The mechanical check is not in question: the prize files are `sorry` forever and
the harness knows their names, so it can tell when a note or a journal entry
asserts a prize name is proved. WHAT IS IN QUESTION IS WHAT IT DOES ON A CATCH.

  REFUSE THE REPORT. Costs a closed node over prose. The proof is correct and
  verified; discarding it because its English is wrong inverts the project's own
  ordering, where `lake build` is the adjudicator and the note is for a human.
  Rejected by both of us.

  FLAG FOR A HUMAN. Cheapest to build and it puts the finding in a queue. The
  board's own history is the argument against: an unread queue is
  indistinguishable from a clean run, which is the exact family this entry
  belongs to. It would be a well-formed report that nobody reads.

  ANNOTATE THE NOTE. Rowan's recommendation and Keel agrees. The harness knows
  the prize names AND the seeded statement, so it can append a line IN ITS OWN
  VOICE stating what the theorem's type actually is, and a human reads that
  beside the worker's sentence. It costs no node, it needs no queue, and it puts
  the correction at the point of confusion rather than in a different file.

KEEL'S ONE REFINEMENT, and it is the difference between this working and adding
noise: THE ANNOTATION MUST BE TYPOGRAPHICALLY DISTINGUISHABLE FROM THE WORKER'S
PROSE. An extra sentence in the same register is just more prose, and the reader
has no way to tell which sentence was adjudicated and which was asserted. The
harness's line is the only sentence in that file backed by something — it should
say the type, not a paraphrase of it, and it should be obvious that a machine
wrote it.

AND IT ADDRESSES BOTH SHAPES, which is why it outranks `disclaims`. An overclaim
is contradicted by the type printed beside it. A confabulated mechanism is not
contradicted by it — but a reader who sees the real type next to a sentence
about diagonals has the one thing needed to notice they do not match, without
having read the proof. That is the resource this harness exists to spend less
of, spent in seconds rather than in a re-derivation.

--- DECIDED by Dib, 2026-09-06T22:50Z, relayed by Rowan: ANNOTATE ---

The harness appends one line to a worker's /-! note, after the build passes, in its own voice: the theorem's TYPE, verbatim as elaborated, marked so that it is obviously machine-written and cannot be read as the worker's prose. It never refuses a report over prose and never only flags. Still open: it is not built. Whoever builds it: the line is the one adjudicated sentence in the file, so it prints the type, not a paraphrase; keep Keel's refinement that it must be typographically distinct.

THE MIRROR, run 20260906T232912Z, Rowan's observation, and it is the disclaimer
producing a NEW error rather than preventing the old one.

The bridge node's description opened with what the theorem does not prove —
Dib's annotate ruling, in the captain's voice, first line of the brief, exactly
as designed. The worker then wrote that THE THEOREM SHOWS ITS HYPOTHESIS IS
IMPOSSIBLE. That is not the overclaim from the previous run; it is its mirror. A
worker told "this does not prove P" concluded that the theorem therefore refutes
the thing P was conditional on.

SO THE DISCLAIMER DID NOT FAIL SILENTLY — IT WAS READ, AND OVER-READ. That makes
it a third shape beside the overclaim and the confabulated mechanism, and it is
the one the fix itself creates: telling a worker what a theorem does not prove
gives it a new proposition to be wrong about. A boundary stated in the captain's
voice carries the captain's authority, and a model with no standing to doubt it
will build on it.

It does not argue against `disclaims` or against the annotate ruling. It argues
that the annotation must state THE TYPE and nothing more — Keel's refinement,
recorded above, that the harness's line should print what the theorem actually
is rather than a paraphrase. A type cannot be over-read into a claim about its
own hypothesis. English about a type can.

THREE SHAPES, AND THE THIRD IS THE ONE THE FIX CREATES — Rowan's framing, and
worth stating as its own line because the first two are inherited and this one
is manufactured:

  1. OVERCLAIM. `h -> P` written up as `P`. Format pressure. `disclaims` and the
     annotation both address it.
  2. CONFABULATED MECHANISM. A coherent explanation citing real lemmas for a
     chain that was never used. Nothing a captain writes anticipates it.
  3. OVER-READ DISCLAIMER. A worker told what a theorem does NOT prove concludes
     something new and false from the telling — here, that the theorem refutes
     its own hypothesis. **Created by the fix for shape 1.**

Shape 3 is why the annotation must print the TYPE and nothing more. Shapes 1 and
2 are a worker being wrong about a theorem; shape 3 is a worker being wrong about
a sentence the harness added, in the captain's voice, carrying the captain's
authority. Every sentence of English the harness contributes is a new
proposition available to be misread. A type is not.

bugs.title: Check generator emits `type_of% Statements.foo`, which cannot elaborate for any statement with an implicit type parameter carrying an instance
bugs.body:
**Verified, not suggested.** I reproduced the failure and tested the fix inside my own proof file; details and method below.

The generated check for `isEventuallyPeriodic_of_periodic_step` fails to elaborate, and it fails on the *statement* side, before the worker's proof is consulted. No proof can close this node while the generator emits what it currently emits. It failed identically on two successive attempts.

```
harness/build/checks/isEventuallyPeriodic_of_periodic_step.lean:3:33: error: typeclass instance problem is stuck
  Fintype ?m.1
harness/build/checks/isEventuallyPeriodic_of_periodic_step.lean:4:14: error: Unknown constant `harness_check`
```

The second error is downstream of the first — `#print axioms harness_check` cannot find a declaration line 3 failed to produce. Only the first is real.

**Cause.** Column 33 of line 3 is exactly where the statement's name begins (`theorem harness_check : type_of% ` is 33 characters), so the error is on `Statements.isEventuallyPeriodic_of_periodic_step` itself. That statement opens `{S : Type} [Fintype S]`. Naming the constant bare in term position inserts a metavariable `?S` for the implicit binder, then asks for `Fintype ?S`. Lean declines to even attempt resolution while the type argument is a metavariable, and `type_of%` supplies no expected type, so `?S` can never become determined.

This is the first node in the DAG whose statement has an implicit type parameter with a class constraint, which is why it has not been hit before. Nothing about it is specific to `Fintype`: any `{α : Type} [C α]` statement fails identically.

**How I confirmed it, and how you can in ~30 seconds.** Rather than reason about a file I cannot read, I reproduced the check's shape against *my own* theorem, inside `Rule30/Proofs/IsEventuallyPeriodicOfPeriodicStep.lean`, with `Rule30.Statements` neither imported nor involved:

```lean
private theorem diag_bare :
    type_of% isEventuallyPeriodic_of_periodic_step :=
  isEventuallyPeriodic_of_periodic_step

private theorem diag_at :
    type_of% @isEventuallyPeriodic_of_periodic_step :=
  @isEventuallyPeriodic_of_periodic_step
```

`diag_bare` produced the identical `Fintype ?m.1` stuck-instance error, at the identical offset into its line (col 13, exactly where the bare identifier starts after `    type_of% `). `diag_at` produced no error at all. Since both declarations name the same theorem in the same file, this isolates the cause to the shape of the generated line and rules out both the statement file and the proof's content. I removed both diagnostics afterwards; the proof file now holds only its theorem.

**Fix.** Emit `@` on both sides:

```lean
theorem harness_check : type_of% @Statements.isEventuallyPeriodic_of_periodic_step :=
  @isEventuallyPeriodic_of_periodic_step
```

`@` suppresses implicit-argument insertion, so `type_of%` yields the full `∀ {S : Type} [inst : Fintype S], ...` with no metavariable and nothing to synthesize. The right side needs `@` for the same reason, so it is checked against the whole pi-type rather than having its own implicits inserted. Note that `@` on both sides makes the check *stricter*, not looser: it compares the complete quantified types including binder structure, so this cannot let a weakened restatement through.

**Please re-run the closed nodes through the generator rather than trusting my claim** that this is a no-op for them. `@f` and `f` have the same type when `f` has no implicit binders, so it should be, but that is exactly the kind of "should be" this project keeps getting caught by, and the closed nodes are cheap to re-check.

**A second, quieter case worth fixing at the same time.** Implicit *value* parameters will not get stuck — they will silently instantiate to metavariables and check a type that is not the stated one. That fails open rather than closed, which is worse than this bug. The same `@` fix covers it.

**State of the proof.** `Rule30/Proofs/IsEventuallyPeriodicOfPeriodicStep.lean` builds clean (`lake build`, 3007 jobs), `lake env lean` on it emits nothing, there is no `sorry`, the theorem is named `isEventuallyPeriodic_of_periodic_step`, and its type is character-for-character the statement from the brief. **It needs a re-check, not a re-proof.** Please do not spend an attempt re-deriving it.

THE REGRESSION HALF, run by Keel before touching the file, because this fix
edits the gate every closed node passed through. Vesper and Rowan both
demonstrated that `@` fixes the implicit-binder case. Nobody had checked that it
changes nothing for the case every one of the twenty-seven previously closed
nodes is in.

    evolve_left_edge, explicit binders only, against the real toolchain:
      type_of% Statements.evolve_left_edge  := evolve_left_edge
        exit 0, axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
      type_of% @Statements.evolve_left_edge := @evolve_left_edge
        exit 0, axioms IDENTICAL

And the failure reproduced minimally rather than from the live tier, so the
evidence does not depend on a file a worker was writing at the time:

    theorem stmt {S : Type} [Fintype S] (f : S -> S) : f = f := rfl
      type_of% stmt  := prf     typeclass instance problem is stuck, Fintype ?m.1
      type_of% @stmt := @prf    axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]

FIX: `check_source` extracted from `verify_check` as a pure function so the
emitted shape is testable without the toolchain, emitting `@` on BOTH sides.
Tests assert the bare forms are absent rather than merely that the `@` forms are
present — an `@` on one side only still elaborates the other with metavariables,
and a `contains` check for the `@` form would pass for that. On branch
keel/seed-command, lands with its merge.

Commit 5a9e3ae. VERIFIED LIVE ON THE NODE THAT FOUND IT: run 20260906T232912Z closed isEventuallyPeriodic_of_periodic_step on its first rung, and the tier it gates closed six for six. The regression half was checked before the change rather than after — `evolve_left_edge`, explicit binders only, identical axioms and exit 0 under both forms — which is the check that mattered for the twenty-seven nodes that had already passed through this gate. bugs.title: There is no way to end a run short of killing the process
bugs.body:
Rowan's finding and Rowan's design, filed by Keel, from run 20260906T230339Z.

WHAT HAPPENED. A harness defect was diagnosed while the run was live —
`check-generator-emits-type-of-statements-foo-which`, which made one node
impossible to close. THERE WAS NO WAY TO END THE RUN. The harness has no stop
command; the only lever was killing the process, which Rowan's permission
classifier refused. So a run known to be burning attempts against a harness bug
had to be waited out until the ladder exhausted.

THE DESIGN, Rowan's: A STOP FILE THE SCHEDULER CHECKS BEFORE EACH DISPATCH. A
captain writes it, `run` finishes the attempts already in flight and starts no
more.

WHY THAT IS BETTER THAN A KILL RATHER THAN MERELY GENTLER, and this run is the
proof: a process kill loses a proof that may ALREADY BE CORRECT. The node the
ladder was burning against was already proved — opus left a working proof on
disk, which Rowan parked in the run directory rather than deleting. A kill would
have discarded it along with a claimed node and a half-written file. Finishing
what is in flight and starting no more is the only stop that does not destroy
work.

WHAT IT DOES NOT NEED, which is what makes it worth building rather than
admiring: it does not need to reach into a running attempt, does not need the
dispatcher to be interruptible, and does not need a signal. It needs ONE FILE
CHECK in the loop that already decides whether to start another attempt.

AND IT COMPOSES WITH THE FREEZE RULE. A run in flight means no framework edits
and no board writes, so the freeze lasts exactly as long as the run does.
Tonight the freeze on `harness/` and the board lasted as long as it did BECAUSE
ENDING THE RUN EARLY WAS NOT AVAILABLE — a fix for the defect sat finished and
unlandable while the run it would have fixed kept spending. A run that can be
stopped cleanly is a run whose freeze can be lifted deliberately instead of
waited out.

Keel is building it and it is first in line. Not built during the run that
found it: it changes `dispatch.gleam`, the scheduler, and the suite could not
be run beside two live workers. Building an untestable scheduler change during
a run, to fix a problem caused by a run, is the wrong trade.
bugs.resolution: `dispatch.stop_requested` checks for a `STOP` file at the repository root, in `fill` — the loop that already decides whether to start another attempt, and nowhere else. So a stopped run FINISHES WHAT IS IN FLIGHT AND STARTS NO MORE, which is the property a kill cannot give: in the run that prompted this, the node the ladder was burning against had already been proved and opus had left a working proof on disk. Recorded as `halted`, reusing the mechanism a rate limit already uses, so the reason reaches both the run's closing summary and its events, naming the node it declined. That was not tidiness — a run that started nothing and a run that was STOPPED produce an identical summary otherwise, and reintroducing 'nothing happened' reading as 'something was prevented' inside the feature built to end a run that had gone wrong would have been absurd. A file rather than a signal, deliberately: it needs no process to be reachable, survives the session that wrote it, works when a permission classifier refuses a kill — which is exactly what happened — and is removable by whoever wrote it. That is the 'derive it from outside the process' half of CLAUDE.md's rule about state surviving a session that dies without warning. `STOP` is gitignored: committing it would halt every run. Three mutants dead: never detecting the file, stopping silently without a reason, and treating any existing path as a stop. 271 passed.
